title: The Two Clumsy Men of Cairo and Damascus
summary: There lived in Cairo a well-meaning but hopelessly blunt weaver named Faris, whose tongue was completely devoid of tact. Whenever he spoke, he said the most inappropriate thing ...
keywords: story of the two lack-tacts of cairo and damascus
full_text:
There lived in Cairo a well-meaning but hopelessly blunt weaver named Faris, whose tongue was completely devoid of tact. Whenever he spoke, he said the most inappropriate thing at the worst possible moment.
Visiting a sick friend, he would cheerfully announce: 'Do not worry about the doctor; my uncle died of this exact cough within three days!'
At a wedding, he would remark to the bridegroom: 'Enjoy your youth today, brother, for marriage is a prison of sour vinegar!'

Despairing of finding anyone who understood him, Faris traveled to Damascus, where he heard lived a man of identical temperament named Bashir.
'At last,' thought Faris, 'I shall meet my equal in plain speaking!'

Faris arrived at Bashir's house during the celebration of Bashir's daughter's engagement.
Faris strode into the courtyard, bowed, and announced loudly:
'Peace, friend Bashir! I have traveled from Cairo to congratulate thee on getting rid of thy daughter before her teeth fall out!'

The guests gasped in horror!
Bashir, instead of being offended, stepped forward, embraced Faris, and said with equal lack of tact:
'Welcome, Cairene brother! I see thy nose is as crooked as a camel's knee, and thy traveling coat smells of stale onions!'

The two clumsy men sat together, perfectly pleased with each other, while the entire party fled the courtyard in disgust.
Later, when they walked into the Damascus bazaar, Faris stepped on a baker's basket of hot pies, shouting: 'Thy pies are over-baked anyway!'
Bashir bumped into an armored captain of the municipal guard, yelling: 'Mind your heavy iron scabbard, old soldier, before you rust in the damp air!'

Both craftsmen and soldiers, completely fed up with their unbearable rudeness, grabbed brooms, wet mop-cloths, and dough-rollers, chasing the two clumsy boasters out of the city gates into a muddy ditch!

Sitting in the mire, picking cabbage leaves from their turbans, Faris looked at Bashir and sighed:
'Brother Bashir, perhaps there is a difference between speaking truth and throwing stones with one's tongue.'
Bashir rubbed his bruised elbow and nodded:
'Aye, Faris. A word of courtesy costs nothing, but blunt insolence buys a mud bath every time!'

The two returned to their homes, took vows of silence for forty days, and learned to sweeten their speech with the honey of kindness.
moral: Tact and considerate speech are the oil of human fellowship; heedless bluntness brings endless bruised shins.
